user content licensed to platform royalty-free perpetually

employment_law.topic: Wrongful Termination
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004
employment_law.rule: Under the Nigerian Labour Act, a worker is entitled to minimum notice before termination (1 day for daily workers, 1 week for monthly workers, etc). Summary dismissal is only justified for gross misconduct. Contracts cannot lawfully exclude this right.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure your employment contract specifies at least 1-month notice for senior roles, and clearly defines what constitutes 'gross misconduct' to avoid arbitrary termination.

employment_law.topic: Deduction from Wages
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004, Section 7
employment_law.rule: Deductions from wages are only lawful if authorized by statute, court order, or written agreement with the employee specifying the purpose. Unauthorized deductions constitute a criminal offence under the Labour Act.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Do not sign any clause allowing blanket deductions. Any deduction clause must specify the exact amount, purpose, and your right to dispute.

employment_law.topic: Training Bond / Repayment Clawback
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Nigerian Contract Law
employment_law.rule: Training repayment clauses are only enforceable if: (a) the training expenditure was genuine and documented, (b) the repayment amount is proportionate and reduces pro-rata over time, and (c) the employee was given a meaningful opportunity to negotiate before signing. A flat repayment demand regardless of tenure length is a penalty clause.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Negotiate a declining repayment schedule (e.g., 100% if you leave within 6 months, 50% within 12 months, 0% after 18 months). Insist on seeing the actual training cost receipts before signing any bond.
red_flags: repay all costs if you resign
cost of training shall be recovered

employment_law.topic: Garden Leave / Non-Solicitation
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Restraint of Trade Doctrine
employment_law.rule: Garden leave clauses (requiring the employee to stay away from work during notice while remaining employed) and non-solicitation clauses must be reasonable in duration and scope. Nigerian courts will not enforce them if they effectively prevent a person from working in their profession for an unreasonable period.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Limit garden leave to the actual notice period only. Non-solicitation of clients should be limited to 6 months and restricted to clients you personally dealt with — not the employer's entire client base.
red_flags: may not work during notice period

employment_law.topic: Unilateral Variation of Employment Terms
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004
employment_law.rule: An employer cannot unilaterally vary the fundamental terms of employment (salary, role, location, hours) without the employee's consent. A clause purporting to allow the employer to vary any term at its discretion is void under the Labour Act and equivalent to a repudiatory breach.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure any variation clause requires written agreement from both parties. The employer's ability to vary role or location should be subject to reasonable notice (minimum 30 days) and your right to terminate with full severance if you cannot reasonably accept the variation.
red_flags: employer may modify conditions of employment

employment_law.topic: Excessive Confidentiality / IP Ownership in Employment
employment_law.statute: Copyright Act 2022 & Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004
employment_law.rule: An employment clause assigning all intellectual property created by an employee — including works created in personal time, unrelated to the employer's business — to the employer goes beyond what Nigerian law permits. The Copyright Act 2022 limits employer ownership to works created in the course of employment.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Limit IP assignment to works created 'in the course of employment and using company resources.' Add an explicit carve-out: 'This clause does not apply to works created entirely in the employee's personal time and unrelated to the company's business.'
red_flags: all inventions shall belong to the employer
including works created outside working hours
personal projects shall be company property
all developments belong to the company
intellectual property created at any time
any idea developed is company property

employment_law.topic: Probationary Period Abuse
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Nigerian Employment Practice
employment_law.rule: A probationary period should typically not exceed 3-6 months. Clauses that extend probation indefinitely, reduce notice entitlements to zero during probation, or deny all statutory benefits during an excessively long probation may be void or challengeable.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure probation is capped at 3 months (6 months maximum for senior roles), that at least 1-week notice applies even during probation, and that statutory benefits (pension, leave) accrue from the first day of employment.

employment_law.topic: Pension / Social Security Contribution Evasion
employment_law.statute: Pension Reform Act 2014 (Nigeria) & National Housing Fund Act
employment_law.rule: Under the Pension Reform Act 2014, employers with 3 or more employees must enroll employees in the Contributory Pension Scheme. Employee contribution is 8% of monthly emolument; employer contribution is minimum 10%. A contract that reclassifies employees as independent contractors to avoid pension obligations constitutes illegal pension evasion.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: If your engagement looks like employment (fixed hours, equipment provided, exclusive service), you are entitled to pension contributions regardless of the contract label. Apply to PenCom to enforce pension rights. Employers evading contributions face penalties of 2% per month on outstanding contributions.
red_flags: service provider not entitled to benefits

employment_law.topic: Misclassification of Employees as Independent Contractors
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Pension Reform Act 2014
employment_law.rule: The label 'independent contractor' does not determine actual employment status. Nigerian courts and regulators look at the substance of the relationship: who controls the work, who provides tools, whether there is exclusivity, and whether the worker bears commercial risk. Misclassified employees are denied pension, leave, notice pay, and termination protections.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: If you work exclusively for one business, use their equipment, take instructions on how to work (not just what to deliver), and cannot subcontract your work, you are likely an employee in law. Request employment status determination from PenCom or the National Industrial Court if disputed.
red_flags: your status is that of a contractor
no entitlement to labour act protections
engaged as a vendor not an employee
you provide services as a business

employment_law.topic: Overtime and Rest Period Violations
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004, Sections 13-14
employment_law.rule: The Nigerian Labour Act limits working hours and requires rest periods. An employee cannot waive the right to overtime pay contractually. A clause requiring unlimited hours 'as required by the business' without overtime pay, or that deems ordinary working hours to include overtime, is void.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure your contract specifies a maximum base working week (e.g., 40 hours) and an overtime rate of at least 125% (time and a half) for hours beyond the base. Do not sign clauses that treat 'extended hours' as ordinary time without additional compensation.
red_flags: salary is inclusive of all overtime
hours may be extended without additional pay
flexible hours at employer's discretion with no additional pay

employment_law.topic: Annual Leave Entitlement Waiver
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004, Section 18
employment_law.rule: Under the Nigerian Labour Act, every employee is entitled to a minimum of 6 working days annual leave after 12 months of continuous service (more for senior staff). A clause requiring the employee to waive or 'buy out' statutory annual leave is void.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure your contract specifies annual leave entitlement at or above the statutory minimum. A 'use it or lose it' clause that denies carry-over without any compensation for untaken statutory leave may be challengeable.
red_flags: leave may not be carried over

employment_law.topic: Maternity / Paternity Leave Below Statutory Minimum
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004, Section 54
employment_law.rule: Nigerian law provides a minimum of 12 weeks paid maternity leave for female employees. A contract providing less than 12 weeks, making maternity leave unpaid, or conditioning maternity leave on tenure of more than one year is contrary to the Labour Act.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Insist on a minimum of 12 weeks full-pay maternity leave. Any return-to-work requirement shorter than 8 weeks post-birth is unreasonable. If the company has a paternity leave policy, ensure it is stated in the contract and not merely a discretionary benefit.
red_flags: no right to maternity leave before one year service
maternity leave conditional on service length
maternity leave is a privilege not a right

employment_law.topic: Non-Disparagement / Gagging Clause
employment_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Constitution of Nigeria (Freedom of Expression)
employment_law.rule: A non-disparagement clause prohibiting an employee from making any negative statement about the employer — including truthful statements about unlawful treatment, workplace conditions, or public interest matters — is an unreasonable restraint on freedom of expression and potentially contrary to whistleblower protections under the Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Accept only a mutual, narrow non-disparagement clause limited to false statements of fact and trade secrets. Ensure the clause explicitly excludes truthful statements, regulatory disclosures, court proceedings, and whistleblowing reports to law enforcement.
red_flags: shall not make any negative statement
no right to discuss salary or conditions

employment_law.topic: Overly Broad Post-Employment Non-Compete
employment_law.statute: Nigerian Contract Law & Restraint of Trade Doctrine
employment_law.rule: Post-employment non-compete clauses must be reasonable in time, geographic scope, and the activity restricted to be enforceable in Nigeria. A clause preventing a departing employee from working in their entire professional field for 2-5 years, across Nigeria or globally, is unreasonable and unenforceable as a restraint of trade.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Non-compete duration should not exceed 6-12 months. Geographic scope should match the area where you actually worked. The restricted activity should be specifically defined as working for a direct named competitor, not the entire industry.
red_flags: shall not work in the same industry
may not engage in competing business for 2 years
shall not work for any competitor
shall not be employed in a similar capacity
prohibited from working in the sector

employment_law.topic: Salary in Arrears Beyond One Month
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004
employment_law.rule: Delayed salary payment is unlawful under the Labour Act. A contract providing that salary is payable more than one month in arrears (e.g., 45-day or 60-day payment cycles) transfers financing cost onto the employee. In Nigeria's current inflation environment, delayed salary payment constitutes a material reduction in real compensation.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Insist on monthly salary payment no later than the last working day of the month. Any delay beyond 30 days from the end of the salary month should attract interest at the CBN MPR. Document all salary payment dates to support a Labour Act complaint if payment is repeatedly late.
red_flags: payment of salary by end of following month
salary subject to payroll run cycle
salary disbursed when cash flow permits

employment_law.topic: Illegal Withholding of Certificates and Documents
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Nigerian Common Law
employment_law.rule: An employer who withholds an employee's academic certificates, professional credentials, or personal identity documents as 'security' is engaged in an unlawful act. Such withholding constitutes wrongful detention of personal property and is a tool of economic coercion that Nigerian courts have condemned.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Never surrender original certificates to an employer. If an employer insists, provide certified true copies only. Report the matter to the National Industrial Court if documents are not returned on demand.
red_flags: certificates held pending completion of bond

employment_law.topic: Zero-Hours Contract / Casual Work Abuse
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & ILO Convention No. 175 (Part-Time Work)
employment_law.rule: Contracts that describe an engagement as 'zero-hours' or 'casual' but in practice involve regular, repeated work for a single employer establish an employment relationship with minimum statutory protections regardless of the contract label. Casual workers employed for more than 12 months continuously are entitled to permanent employment protections under the Labour Act.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: If you are called in regularly (even on a 'casual' basis) and have worked for the same employer for more than 12 months, request regularization of your employment with full permanent employee benefits.
red_flags: engagement may be terminated without notice
temporary worker with no permanency rights

employment_law.topic: Health and Safety Waiver
employment_law.statute: Factories Act Cap F1 LFN 2004 & Employees Compensation Act 2010 (Nigeria)
employment_law.rule: An employee cannot contractually waive the right to a safe workplace, compensation for workplace injury, or the protections of the Factories Act and Employees Compensation Act. A clause requiring the employee to acknowledge risk and waive all compensation claims arising from workplace injury is void as contrary to statute and public policy.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Do not sign any clause waiving your right to compensation for workplace injury. Employees in high-risk sectors (construction, oil and gas, manufacturing) should ensure their employer has registered with and paid contributions to the Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) for employee compensation coverage.
red_flags: waives all claims arising from work
disclaimer of employer liability for injury

employment_law.topic: Whistleblower Retaliation Clause
employment_law.statute: Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Act 2000 & Nigerian Labour Act
employment_law.rule: A contract clause that prohibits reporting regulatory violations, fraud, or corrupt practices to government agencies — or that makes continued employment conditional on not reporting — is void as contrary to public policy and the ICPC Act. Retaliation against a whistleblower is itself a criminal offence under Nigerian law.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Do not sign any clause that restricts your right to report suspected fraud, corruption, or regulatory violations to ICPC, EFCC, CBN, or other regulators. If you are pressured not to report wrongdoing as a condition of employment or settlement, this itself constitutes obstruction of justice.
red_flags: confidential matter not to be disclosed to authorities
waives right to report suspected fraud

employment_law.topic: Secondment / Inter-Company Transfer Without Consent
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap L1 LFN 2004 & Nigerian Contract Law
employment_law.rule: Seconding an employee to a different legal entity (e.g., a subsidiary, affiliate, or client) without the employee's written consent, and without preserving their employment terms and length of service, can result in loss of continuity of employment and statutory benefits. The secondee remains employed by the original employer and retains all accrued rights.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Ensure any secondment agreement: (a) confirms your original employer remains your employer of record, (b) preserves your continuity of service, (c) specifies the secondment duration and return date, and (d) confirms your original terms apply throughout, with any additional allowances specified.

employment_law.topic: West Africa — Ghana Employment Act Protections
employment_law.statute: Labour Act 2003 (Act 651) (Ghana) & National Pensions Act 2008 (Act 766) (Ghana)
employment_law.rule: Ghana's Labour Act (Act 651) provides: minimum 15 working days annual leave, 3 months paid maternity leave (full pay for first 5 years, 2/3 pay thereafter), minimum notice period of one month for monthly-paid workers, and protection from unfair termination through the National Labour Commission. All employers with 5 or more workers must register with the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT).
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In Ghana, ensure your employer is registered with SSNIT and making contributions. Your employer contributes 13% of basic salary to SSNIT, you contribute 5.5%. Challenge any contract providing less than 15 working days annual leave or 3 months maternity leave as contrary to Act 651.
red_flags: annual leave of 10 days in ghana
maternity leave of 6 weeks in ghana
termination before national labour commission approval

employment_law.topic: East Africa — Kenya Employment Act Minimum Standards
employment_law.statute: Employment Act 2007 (Kenya) & Work Injury Benefits Act 2007 (Kenya)
employment_law.rule: Kenya's Employment Act 2007 provides: minimum 21 working days annual leave, 3 months paid maternity leave, 2 weeks paid paternity leave, minimum 28-day notice for termination after one month service, written contract required for all employees, and written reasons for dismissal are mandatory. Unfair dismissal can be referred to the Employment and Labour Relations Court.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In Kenya, insist on a written contract regardless of employment term. Ensure your contract specifies the NSSF and NHIF contributions. Challenge any dismissal where you were not given a fair hearing before a panel — procedural fairness is a legal requirement under the Employment Act.
red_flags: annual leave of 15 days in kenya
no right to hearing before dismissal
casual employment with no rights in kenya
dismissal without written reasons in kenya

employment_law.topic: East Africa — Tanzania and Uganda Employment Protections
employment_law.statute: Employment and Labour Relations Act 2004 (Tanzania) & Employment Act 2006 (Uganda)
employment_law.rule: In Tanzania, the Employment and Labour Relations Act requires minimum 28 days annual leave, 84 days paid maternity leave, and referral of unfair termination to the Commission for Mediation and Arbitration (CMA). In Uganda, the Employment Act 2006 requires minimum 21 days annual leave, 60 days paid maternity leave, and termination with fair reasons and procedure. Employers must register with NSSF in both countries.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In Tanzania, unfair dismissal must be referred to the CMA within 30 days. In Uganda, challenge any dismissal without 'fair reason' (capability, conduct, redundancy) before the Industrial Court. Both countries prohibit waiver of statutory minimum benefits in employment contracts.
red_flags: annual leave below 28 days in tanzania
maternity leave below 84 days in tanzania
annual leave below 21 days in uganda
maternity leave below 60 days in uganda
termination without fair procedure in uganda

employment_law.topic: Southern Africa — South Africa Unfair Dismissal and Labour Relations
employment_law.statute: Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 & Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 (South Africa)
employment_law.rule: Under South Africa's Labour Relations Act, every dismissal must be procedurally and substantively fair. An employee may refer an unfair dismissal to the CCMA within 30 days. Employment contracts cannot contract out of LRA protections. The Employment Equity Act prohibits unfair discrimination and requires designated employers to implement equity plans.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: South African employees: do not sign any clause waiving your right to refer disputes to the CCMA or Labour Court. Probation periods cannot exceed 6 months, and dismissal during probation must still follow a fair procedure.
red_flags: dismissal at will in south africa
probation may be extended beyond 6 months
summary dismissal during probation in south africa
no right to hearing before dismissal

employment_law.topic: Southern Africa — Zimbabwe and Zambia Labour Protections
employment_law.statute: Labour Act Cap 28:01 (Zimbabwe) & Employment Code Act 2019 (Zambia)
employment_law.rule: In Zimbabwe, the Labour Act requires that retrenchment (redundancy) be approved by the National Employment Council or Labour Court, and employees are entitled to retrenchment packages. In Zambia, the Employment Code Act 2019 provides 30 days minimum notice and retrenchment benefits equal to one month's pay per year of service. Contracts in both countries cannot waive these statutory minimums.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In Zimbabwe, any retrenchment without NEC approval is invalid. In Zambia, ensure your contract specifies retrenchment benefits in accordance with the Employment Code Act 2019. Both countries' courts have reversed employer-imposed waiver clauses as contrary to statute.
red_flags: notice of less than 30 days in zambia

employment_law.topic: Europe — UK Employment Zero-Hours Worker Rights
employment_law.statute: Employment Rights Act 1996 (UK) & Workers (Predictable Terms and Conditions) Act 2023 (UK)
employment_law.rule: In the UK, zero-hours workers are 'workers' (not employees) with rights to: national minimum wage, 5.6 weeks paid holiday, rest breaks, and protection from unlawful wage deduction. Exclusivity clauses in zero-hours contracts (requiring the worker to work only for one employer) are unenforceable under the Employment Rights Act 1996. After 26 weeks, workers may request predictable working hours under the 2023 Act.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: UK zero-hours workers: exclusivity clauses are void — you may work for multiple employers. You are entitled to accrue holiday at 12.07% of hours worked. Request a fixed-hours contract after 26 weeks under the Workers (Predictable Terms and Conditions) Act 2023.
red_flags: may only work for one employer
zero hours worker has no employment rights
zero hours worker no sick pay

employment_law.topic: Europe — EU Fixed-Term Contract Renewal Abuse
employment_law.statute: EU Fixed-Term Work Directive 1999/70/EC & Various EU Member State implementing legislation
employment_law.rule: EU law prohibits the abusive use of successive fixed-term employment contracts. After a maximum number of renewals or years of service (varying by member state — typically 2-3 renewals or 2-3 years), successive fixed-term contracts must convert to permanent employment. Employers who renew fixed-term contracts repeatedly to avoid permanent employment obligations are in breach of EU law.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In EU jurisdictions, track your total period of fixed-term employment. In Germany, fixed-term contracts cannot exceed 2 years total (with max 3 renewals) without objective justification. In France, fixed-term contracts convert to permanent (CDI) after the maximum fixed-term period. Challenge renewal of a fixed-term contract beyond the statutory maximum as unlawful.

employment_law.topic: North America — US Non-Compete and NDA Overreach
employment_law.statute: FTC Non-Compete Rule (2024, under litigation) & State law (varies significantly by state)
employment_law.rule: The US Federal Trade Commission issued a rule in 2024 banning most employee non-competes (subject to ongoing legal challenges). California, Colorado, Minnesota, and Oklahoma have separately banned employee non-competes entirely by state law. Even in states where non-competes are enforceable, courts blue-pencil (reduce) unreasonable duration, geography, or scope. NDAs that prevent reporting of crimes or regulatory violations are prohibited under the Speak Out Act 2022 for harassment and assault matters.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In California: any non-compete is void regardless of what it says. In other US states: non-competes must be narrowly tailored, supported by consideration, and reasonable in scope. Do not sign NDAs that purport to prohibit reporting of crimes to law enforcement — these are void under the Speak Out Act for harassment matters and likely void on public policy grounds for other crimes.
red_flags: nda covering all information ever disclosed
broad nda with no time limit
nda waiving right to report crimes

employment_law.topic: North America — Canada Provincial Employment Standards
employment_law.statute: Employment Standards Act 2000 (Ontario) & Canada Labour Code (Federal jurisdiction)
employment_law.rule: Canadian employment standards vary by province and between federally and provincially regulated sectors. Ontario's ESA 2000 provides: minimum 2 weeks vacation (rising to 3 weeks after 5 years), minimum termination notice of 1-8 weeks (plus severance pay for 5+ years), and limits on hours of work. Contracts cannot provide less than ESA minimums. The duty to accommodate disability and protected grounds is governed by the Ontario Human Rights Code.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In Canada, identify whether your employer is federally or provincially regulated. Federally regulated employees (banks, telecom, airlines) are covered by the Canada Labour Code, which is generally more protective. Province-specific ESAs set the floor — any contract term below the ESA minimum is automatically void.
red_flags: termination with 1 week notice in canada

employment_law.topic: Asia — India Employment Protections and Labour Law Compliance
employment_law.statute: Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (India) & Code on Wages 2019 & Factories Act 1948 (India)
employment_law.rule: Indian labour law is split across multiple central and state laws, now being consolidated under four Labour Codes (Wages, IR, Social Security, Occupational Safety). Key protections: minimum wage (state-specific); no termination of workers in establishments with 100+ employees without government approval; gratuity of 15 days pay per year of service after 5 years; 12 days paid casual leave; 26 weeks paid maternity leave. Contracts cannot waive these rights.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: In India, verify the applicable minimum wage for your skill category and state. Gratuity is a statutory entitlement after 5 years of continuous service — do not waive this in any separation agreement. For establishments with 100+ workers, retrenchment without government approval is void.
red_flags: maternity leave below 26 weeks in india
retrenchment without industrial dispute act compliance

employment_law.topic: Asia — Middle East Domestic Worker Kafala System Traps
employment_law.statute: UAE Labour Law Federal Decree No. 33 of 2021 & ILO Convention No. 189 (Domestic Workers)
employment_law.rule: The kafala (sponsorship) system in Gulf countries (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman) historically tied a migrant worker's legal status to their employer/sponsor, making it practically impossible to change employers or leave the country without the employer's permission. While reforms are underway in Qatar (2020) and UAE (2021) to allow job mobility without employer consent, kafala-adjacent practices persist — including: contract substitution (a different contract substituted on arrival), document confiscation, and exit ban clauses.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Before accepting Gulf employment: verify the signed contract is in English and Arabic and identical to the contract you will sign on arrival. Confirm the right to change employers after one year without sponsor consent (now legal in UAE and Qatar). Never surrender your passport to an employer — this is illegal across all GCC states. Register any employment dispute with the Ministry of Human Resources (UAE) or ADLSA (Qatar).
red_flags: cannot leave country without employer permission
employer consent required to change jobs
contract may differ from original offer

employment_law.topic: Global — Migrant Worker Recruitment Fee Exploitation
employment_law.statute: ILO Forced Labour Convention 1930 (No. 29) & ILO Protocol 2014 & Nigerian Labour Act
employment_law.rule: The ILO's Employer Pays Principle (EPP) establishes that no worker should pay for their own recruitment. Recruitment fees charged to migrant workers — for visas, flights, medical tests, training, or agent fees — create debt bondage that constitutes a form of forced labour under the ILO Forced Labour Convention. Nigerian recruitment agencies that charge workers for overseas placement fees may violate the Labour Act and trafficking laws.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Legitimate overseas employment never requires the worker to pay a recruitment fee. Report any recruitment agency demanding fees from workers to the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP). Verify any overseas job offer through the Nigerian Embassy in the destination country before paying anything.
red_flags: medical test fee charged to worker

employment_law.topic: Global — Remote Work / Cross-Border Employment Compliance Risk
employment_law.statute: Nigerian Labour Act & Various National Tax and Immigration Laws
employment_law.rule: A Nigerian employee working remotely for a foreign employer, or a foreign employee working remotely from Nigeria, creates complex tax, social security, and immigration compliance issues in both jurisdictions. Many cross-border remote work arrangements are structured to benefit the employer by avoiding Nigerian labour law protections and pension obligations, or the employee by avoiding personal income tax registration in Nigeria.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: For remote work arrangements: confirm which country's labour law and tax law applies. Insist on a written employment contract specifying the applicable law. Verify that PAYE (Pay-As-You-Earn) income tax is being remitted in the correct jurisdiction. If the employer is foreign, confirm Nigerian pension (RSA) contributions are being made if you are Nigerian and working in Nigeria.
red_flags: remote work with no labour law specified
paid via foreign entity to avoid tax
salary paid to foreign account to avoid nigerian tax

employment_law.topic: Global — Settlement Agreement Coercion and Full and Final Settlement Traps
employment_law.statute: Nigerian Labour Act & Common Law
employment_law.rule: Settlement agreements in which an employee waives all future claims against the employer in exchange for a payment must be entered into voluntarily and with full knowledge of the rights being waived. A settlement agreement signed under duress (e.g., the employee was told to 'sign or be dismissed'), without independent legal advice, or that purports to waive statutory rights (pension, minimum notice, maternity leave) is challengeable.
employment_law.negotiation_tip: Never sign a full and final settlement agreement without: (a) a minimum 7 days to consider it, (b) independent legal advice (which the employer should pay for), and (c) a clear statement of what statutory claims are being waived. Statutory claims that cannot be waived by agreement — such as pension contributions and NSITF claims — should be excluded from any waiver.
red_flags: no right to appeal after signing
settlement agreement must be signed today
